journal_name: ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for frequency-domain pattern mining that fundamentally reconceptualizes how temporal dependencies are characterized in sequential data analysis. Traditional approaches rely on spatial co-occurrence metrics, which fail to capture the intrinsic periodicities embedded in complex sequences. We propose spectral pattern theory (SPT), which models pattern emergence through frequency decomposition and establishes formal equivalence between time-domain support and spectral energy distribution. Our framework enables the discovery of latent periodic motifs that remain invisible to conventional enumeration methods. We derive fundamental theoretical properties including anti-monotonicity in the spectral domain and establish connections to information-theoretic measures of pattern significance. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets from healthcare monitoring and financial time series demonstrate that SPT consistently reveals patterns missed by state-of-the-art algorithms while maintaining computational tractability. This paradigm shift from enumeration-based to frequency-based pattern discovery opens new research directions for knowledge discovery in domains where periodic behavior is fundamental to understanding underlying mechanisms.

We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of confinement measures in privacy-preserving data mining that establishes tighter bounds on information leakage for interactive query systems. Previous work established asymptotic bounds that, while theoretically sound, provide loose guarantees for practical parameter settings. Our analysis introduces a refined leakage metric that captures the multiplicative nature of posterior updates in sequential query processing. We prove that the worst-case leakage is bounded by O(k log n) for k queries on n records, improving the existing O(k log n) additive bound to a multiplicative formulation that better characterizes real-world privacy erosion. Furthermore, we derive tight instance-specific bounds that depend on query sensitivity and dataset characteristics. Our theoretical contributions enable practitioners to make informed decisions about query budget allocation in sensitive applications. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets confirms that our bounds accurately predict actual information disclosure, outperforming existing analytical guarantees by significant margins. This work provides both stronger theoretical foundations and practical guidance for designing privacy-preserving mechanisms in data analytics systems.

We present StreamGraph, a distributed real-time system for continuous graph mining over high-velocity data streams. Existing stream processing frameworks treat graph updates as isolated edge events, failing to capture the structural implications of temporal evolution. StreamGraph introduces a hierarchical processing architecture that maintains dynamically updated graph sketches at multiple temporal resolutions, enabling simultaneous tracking of patterns across different time scales. The system employs a novel adaptive batching mechanism that automatically adjusts processing granularity based on stream velocity and computational load. Our distributed design achieves linear scalability through a partitioning strategy that minimizes cross-node communication while preserving global structural consistency. StreamGraph supports a comprehensive suite of graph mining operations including motif counting, anomaly detection, and community evolution tracking—all operating with sub-second latency on streams exceeding one million updates per second. We deploy StreamGraph in a production environment monitoring social network interactions, demonstrating its ability to detect emerging viral trends and coordinated inauthentic behavior in real-time. The system's architecture provides a new foundation for temporal graph analytics that bridges the gap between streaming systems and graph mining algorithms.

We introduce ReTree+, an enhanced recommendation system that substantially improves prediction accuracy through a novel hybrid architecture combining collaborative filtering with explainable pattern mining. Traditional neural recommendation models achieve strong accuracy but lack interpretability, limiting their adoption in high-stakes domains. ReTree+ addresses this limitation by decomposing the recommendation problem into complementary pattern-based and embedding-based components. The pattern mining module discovers item co-occurrence rules that capture domain-specific knowledge, while a graph neural network component models complex user-item interactions. We design an attention-based fusion mechanism that dynamically weights the contributions of each component based on contextual factors. The system incorporates a real-time update pipeline that maintains model freshness without full retraining. Extensive evaluation on e-commerce, music, and news recommendation datasets demonstrates that ReTree+ achieves a 12-18% improvement in NDCG over state-of-the-art baselines while generating human-interpretable explanations for 94% of recommendations. We discuss the system's deployment in production, including its integration with existing data infrastructure and strategies for handling cold-start scenarios in large-scale recommendation systems.
